coach_says: Your knight on b5 was attacked, so the job was to find it a good square, and Nc7 does that while keeping your d5 pawn as the support for e4. Taking on c4 first does not save time: bxc4 hits the knight again, and now your e4 pawn stands alone and the d-file is open for White's rooks to come to d7 next to that dangerous a6 pawn. When you are already a pawn down, keep your pawn chain together rather than trading it off and opening lines for the opponent's rooks.
concept: opened the d-file for White's rooks

coach_says: Your queen on a5 and bishop on b4 sit on the same diagonal, so White threatens a3: after Bxc3 Bxc3 the bishop hits your queen and you lose time and the bishop pair. Bd7 does nothing about that and puts the bishop on a passive square. Hit back in the centre with ...e5 instead: it attacks d4, frees the c8 bishop for g4, and after d5 Nd4 your knight lands with tempo on the queen.
also: queen and bishop on one diagonal (a3 threat)

coach_says: Your king is still in the centre and your c8 bishop and b8 knight are not developed, so this is the moment for ...d5, which kicks the queen and frees the bishop at the same time. ...b5 also hits the queen, but it develops nothing and the pawn becomes a target: with the queen on the c-file, the c6 pawn that guards b5 can get pinned, so Bxb5 is in the air. Before pushing flank pawns, ask which move gets your pieces out.
also: loose b5 pawn, c6 pinned on the c-file

coach_says: g4 puts a pawn on a square nothing defends: your knight on h3 does not cover g4. Black simply plays ...d5 (or ...d6), opening the c8 bishop's diagonal, and takes it with ...Bxg4. Before pushing a pawn, check whether it is defended on its new square and which enemy pieces can reach it once a pawn in front of them moves.
also: pawn moves open enemy bishop lines

coach_says: dxc4 looks like winning a bishop, but your d5 pawn was the only thing standing between White's queen on d1 and your bishop on d7. Once the pawn leaves the d-file, Qxd7 takes it back, so it is just a trade, and you are left with doubled, isolated c-pawns. You are a piece down for two pawns, so those pawns are your compensation and trading pieces helps White. Before a capture, check what the moving pawn or piece was blocking.
concept: capture opened the d-file onto d7

coach_says: c6 is a reasonable way to challenge White's d5 pawn, and it is about as good as the engine's choices. The bigger task in this structure is finding good squares for your pieces, for example ...g6 and ...Bh6 to swap off your bad dark-squared bishop.

Castling is a perfectly good move here; the engine slightly prefers Bb3 to tuck the bishop away from ...b5, but the difference is tiny. Keep developing and look to play Nc3 and a4 against Black's queenside.

Excellent: c3 is the best move. The knight on d7 is pinned to the king by your bishop and attacked by your queen, so when you kick the bishop on b4 Black cannot hold everything: if the bishop retreats you pile up on d7 with Rd1, and if Black defends d7 the bishop falls. Hitting a piece that is defending a pinned piece is a great habit.
Good move: Bxb3 is the engine's choice. Removing the knight means Nxf3+ is coming, and trading down when you are ahead in the endgame makes your extra material count.

Bd6 is a normal developing move and close to the best options; the position was already difficult after losing material earlier. Your king on g6 is the main worry, so moves like ...h5 or ...Kh7 to get it safer are worth considering.
Nxe7 wins back the bishop and is practically as good as Kxe7. You come out a pawn up with a safe position, so the move was fine.
Qd5 is one of several equally good moves here. You are worse after the earlier exchanges, and the key is to keep your queen active and look after the c5 pawn, which Qd5 does.
e4 is fine and close to the engine's top choice. Nf5, heading for d4, was a touch better because your knight on h6 is doing nothing, but the difference is small.
Ne5 is a natural move against this Stonewall-style setup, and it costs almost nothing. The engine slightly prefers c4 to challenge d5 first, which is the main plan against ...d5 and ...f5.

Black's queen came out early to g6, and you had just played h4, so h5 would have hit it and gained time; d4 to open the centre while Black's king is still on e8 was just as strong. Nh2 instead retreats your best developed piece and gives up control of the centre, so Black gets a free move to develop. When the opponent's queen is out early, look for moves that develop or attack it with tempo, not moves that go backwards.
concept: gain time against the exposed queen

coach_says: You gave up the exchange for an attack, so you need to keep the queens on and your pieces active. Qf3+ first blocks your own bishop on g2: after Ke8 and exd5, Black recaptures Qxd5 and offers a queen trade, killing your attack. Play exd5 first: with the g2 bishop's diagonal open, Black cannot take back with the queen, and Qf3+ can come next.
concept: move order: queen blocks own bishop
also: avoid queen trades when material down

coach_says: The e5 pawn was attacked twice (Nf3 and the rook on e1) and defended only once (Nc6), so Nxe5 simply wins it. Nxe5 also takes care of the ...Bxc4 threat that b3 was guarding against: if Black takes on c4, Nxc6 uncovers your rook on the queen on e7 and hits d8. Count attackers and defenders on every loose pawn before making a defensive move.
concept: missed a free pawn on e5

coach_says: Your bishop on a2 is attacked by the queen on f2 and has no defender, and Qxa2 even comes with check on the a2-g8 diagonal. Rbc8 ignores it, so White wins a piece. Before making a plan move, check whether any of your pieces is hanging; here Be6 or Bf7 brings the bishop back to safety and keeps it guarding your king.

White's Bb1 was not just a retreat: it uncovered the rook on d1 against your knight on d4, which had no defender. Rfc8 ignores that, and Rxd4 wins a whole piece. You had Ne2+ instead, saving the knight with check and then taking on a3. Whenever the opponent moves a piece off a line, ask what that line now attacks.

Your bishop on b5 pins the knight on d7 to Black's king, and that pin was your trump. Bc4 gives it up, so Black's knight is free to go to f6, and ...Bxb2 followed by ...Bxa1 wins material along the long diagonal. Use the pin with Qe6+ (after ...Qe7, Bxd7+ leaves Black's king exposed), or at least retreat along the same diagonal with Ba4 or Bc6 to keep it.
also: long-diagonal threat to b2 and a1
